story.e: The Philistines gathered for war against Israel, and the two armies camped facing each other with a valley between them. From the Philistines stepped out a giant, Goliath of Gath. He had a bronze helmet on his head, scale armour on his body, and the shaft of his spear was as thick as the beam of a loom. Morning and evening he stepped out and called: “Choose a man from among you and let him come down to me! If he defeats me, we will be your servants; if I defeat him, you will be ours.” He did this for forty days, and Saul and all Israel were terrified. David was still at home with the flock. His father sent him to take food to his brothers, who were serving as soldiers. When he arrived he heard Goliath’s shout and saw everyone running away. David asked: “Who is this, that he insults the army of the living God?” His eldest brother grew angry with him: “Why did you come here? I know you only wanted to see the battle.” David answered: “What have I done? I only asked.” They took him to Saul, and David said: “Let no one lose heart: your servant will go and fight this Philistine.” Saul answered: “You cannot go, for you are still young, and he has been a warrior from his youth.” David told him that as a shepherd he had faced a lion and a bear when they carried off a lamb from the flock: “The Lord, who saved me from the claws of the lion and the bear, will save me from the hand of this Philistine too.” Saul put his own armour on him, but David could not walk in it: “I am not used to this.” He took it off, picked up his staff, chose five smooth stones from the stream, and went out with his sling. Goliath despised him: “Am I a dog, that you come at me with a stick?” David answered: “You come against me with sword, spear and javelin, but I come in the name of the Lord of Hosts. The Lord does not save by sword and spear: the battle is his.” When the Philistine moved towards him, David ran quickly, took a stone from his bag, slung it, and struck him on the forehead. Goliath fell face down on the ground. The Philistines fled.
story.m: The Philistines gathered their armies for war, and Israel also drew up in battle order: the two camps faced each other with a valley between them. Then a champion stepped out from the Philistine camp, Goliath of Gath, whose height was six cubits and a span. He had a bronze helmet on his head, scale armour of bronze on his body, bronze guards on his legs and a bronze javelin on his shoulder; the shaft of his spear was like a weaver’s beam, and its iron point weighed several kilos. His shield-bearer went before him. Goliath stood and shouted to the ranks of Israel: “Why have you come out to draw up in battle order? Am I not the Philistine, and you the servants of Saul? Choose a man from among you and let him come down to me! If he can fight me and defeat me, we will be your servants; but if I defeat him, you will be our servants.” And he added: “Today I defy the ranks of Israel: give me a man, that we may fight each other!” Saul and all Israel were dismayed and greatly afraid at these words. For forty days the Philistine came out every morning and evening and shouted the same. David at this time was still at home in Bethlehem keeping his father’s flock; his three eldest brothers, however, were serving in Saul’s army. One day his father Jesse sent him: “Take your brothers roasted grain and bread, and cheese to their commander, and see how they are.” David rose early, left the flock with a keeper, and set out. When he reached the camp, the army was just marching out into battle order with a war cry. David ran to the ranks, greeted his brothers, and while he was speaking with them the Philistine stepped out and spoke his usual words; David heard this too. And the men of Israel, when they saw the Philistine, fled from him in great fear. David asked those standing beside him: “What will be done for the man who kills this Philistine and takes away the disgrace from Israel? For who is this uncircumcised Philistine, that he insults the army of the living God?” When his eldest brother Eliab heard what he was saying to the men, he grew angry with him and said: “Why did you come here? With whom did you leave those few sheep in the wilderness? I know your recklessness and the wickedness of your heart: you only came to see the battle.” David answered: “What have I done now? It was only a word!” When his words were reported to Saul, the king summoned him. David said to him: “Let no one lose heart because of this man: your servant will go and fight this Philistine.” Saul answered: “You cannot go out to fight him, for you are still young, and he has been a warrior from his youth.” But David said: “Your servant was keeping his father’s sheep, and when a lion or a bear came and carried off a lamb from the flock, I went after it, struck it down and snatched the lamb from its mouth. The Lord, who saved me from the claws of the lion and the bear, will save me from the hand of this Philistine too.” Then Saul said: “Go, and may the Lord be with you!” And he put his own armour on him: he set a bronze helmet on his head and put a coat of armour on him. David also strapped on the sword and tried to walk in it, but he could not, for he was not used to it. So he said to Saul: “I cannot walk in these, for I am not used to them.” He took them off, picked up his staff, chose five smooth stones from the stream, put them in his shepherd’s bag, and with his sling in his hand went towards the Philistine. The Philistine also came on, with his shield-bearer before him. When he saw David he despised him, for he was young and ruddy. He said to him: “Am I a dog, that you come at me with a stick?” And he cursed David by his gods. David answered: “You come against me with sword, spear and javelin, but I come against you in the name of the Lord of Hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have insulted. The whole earth will know that there is a God in Israel, and all this assembly will know that the Lord does not save by sword and spear: for the battle is the Lord’s.” When the Philistine set out and drew near to David, David ran quickly towards the battle line to meet him. He reached into his bag, took out a stone, slung it, and struck the Philistine on the forehead; the stone sank into his forehead, and he fell face down on the ground. So David proved stronger than the Philistine with a sling and a stone. When the Philistines saw that their champion had fallen, they fled.
story.h: This is one of the best-known stories in the Bible, and for that very reason it is worth reading carefully, because it says almost everything differently from the way we tend to remember it. Four things are worth seeing apart. The first is single combat as an institution. Goliath is not simply making threats: he is proposing a custom of the time in which two armies settle a battle through their best fighters, so that thousands need not die. It is therefore a legally valid offer, and for forty days Israel can do nothing with it. In the Bible forty days is usually the span of a testing — the same number as the wilderness wandering or the fast. The second, almost always left out: David is not a volunteer hero but a little brother sent to deliver food. The text describes the provisions in detail, and also that he left the flock with a keeper — he did not abandon his duty either. When he speaks, it is his own brother who humiliates him: “I know the wickedness of your heart.” The family does not believe in him, even though it was in this very family, in chapter 16, that he was anointed. The third is the armour scene, the chapter’s hidden centre. Saul offers his own armour — and note what that means: the king is the tallest man in Israel and David is the youngest son. The armour literally does not fit. David’s sentence — “I am not used to this” — is not only practical: it also means he will not win by the king’s method. Whoever goes out in Saul’s armour fights Saul’s battle; David instead takes what he knows: the shepherd’s staff and the sling. The sling, by the way, was no child’s toy but a ranged weapon of the period with which a practised hand could aim very accurately — David is therefore not reckless; he fights with his own strength. The fourth is the chapter’s real claim, spoken by David before the fight: “the Lord does not save by sword and spear.” This does not mean preparation is pointless — David chooses five stones, not one, and he runs rather than waits. It means the outcome does not depend on the size of the weapons. And there is one small detail that lights up the whole story: Goliath measures everyone by his own standard, and so does not take seriously anyone who comes differently. That is exactly the fault the people committed when they chose the tallest man as king.
